title: Issue 2 Cover — Dead Weight in the Basin
summary: Cover for Sunforge Outlaw Issue 2, “Dead Weight in the Basin.” Sell the pressure of an itinerant community trying to put Brandon into the absent General’s chair. The cover should feel like a Western standoff conducted through expectation rather than gunfire. Dominant hook: Everyone at the table is waiting for Brandon to become General Diaz. Emotional promise: social pressure, dry humor, frontier politics, and another identity that fits too specifically.
settingText: Cinder Basin traveling camp beneath black half-buried Sunforge ribs; communal table, patched shade, heat and ochre dust.
panelPlan: Single full-bleed portrait comic cover. No interior panel grid, no recap montage, no character-lineup poster, and no process or infographic framing.

Dominant selling image: A communal table divides the lower half of the cover into two opposed clusters of Los Lagartos. At the head is one conspicuously empty practical camp chair associated with the absent General. Brandon stands just behind or beside that chair rather than sitting in it, visually refusing the role while every eyeline converges on him. The black Sunforge ribs arc above the camp like old bones without becoming mystical.
Symbolic logic: The empty chair is the identity everyone wants Brandon to occupy; his refusal to sit is more important than any weapon.

Thumbnail rule: the cover must still read at small size through one dominant silhouette or object relationship, a simple large-value composition, and a single obvious focal path. Do not depend on tiny props, background faces, or environmental lettering to explain the hook.

Trade-dress rule: reserve clean, intentional negative space for the established Sunforge Outlaw masthead, issue-number system, and any title treatment carried by the approved Issue 1 cover. Do not let important faces, hands, or the central symbolic object sit beneath the masthead zone.
Spoiler ceiling: Do not depict the later violent intervention, Brandon’s argument that the group must choose without Diaz, Raina’s investigation, or the preacher clue.
Must include: empty General’s place; Brandon visibly outside the assigned role; divided community around one table; hard basin light and black Sunforge ribs.
Must avoid: throne imagery; military-general costume on Brandon; gunfight spectacle; Raina reveal; mystical glow.

title: Issue 3 Cover — A Shadow on the Glass
summary: Cover for Sunforge Outlaw Issue 3, “A Shadow on the Glass.” Sell a refuge built on not asking names just as Brandon’s presence makes one old identity impossible to ignore. Dominant hook: A place where nobody asks who you are recognizes Brandon anyway. Emotional promise: intimacy, accusation, mirrored identity, and the sense that the planted story has found a wound it should not know.
settingText: Mirage Club threshold: brutal white Sunfields daylight above street level, narrow stair into cool dark interior, reflective glass and worn club surfaces.
panelPlan: Single full-bleed portrait comic cover. No interior panel grid, no recap montage, no character-lineup poster, and no process or infographic framing.

Dominant selling image: Use a strong vertical split between white exterior glare and the cool club below. Brandon descends or stands at the threshold while a sheet of dark glass or mirror catches a second, slightly displaced reflection of him. Isabella is inside the shadowed club, small but unmistakably focused on him. The cover should feel like recognition occurring across a boundary rather than a confrontation pose.
Symbolic logic: The reflective surface makes one face carry two possible histories without confirming either one.

Thumbnail rule: the cover must still read at small size through one dominant silhouette or object relationship, a simple large-value composition, and a single obvious focal path. Do not depend on tiny props, background faces, or environmental lettering to explain the hook.

Must include: daylight-to-shadow contrast; Brandon doubled by reflection; Mirage Club as refuge rather than den of villains; Isabella’s recognition pressure.
Must avoid: two literal Brandons; ghost imagery; holograms; readable club signage; revealing Merritt as true.

Behind her, a family ledger and keys rest on a chair or worktable—the responsibility waiting for her. The open road is visible beyond the yard. Brandon is present only as a small background figure doing ordinary work and receiving no special attention.

title: Issue 8 Cover — The Farther Rider
summary: Cover for Sunforge Outlaw Issue 8, “The Farther Rider.” Make distance itself the unsettling object. This is the first cover allowed to lean into the uncanny, but it must remain visually honest and physically grounded. Dominant hook: A tiny rider on a far white ridge is too distant to matter and too precisely placed to ignore. Emotional promise: frontier scale, observational dread, and the first phenomenon that resists the human explanations.
settingText: The Long Mile beneath an enormous bleached sky; pale ridge systems, hard dry road, almost no visual clutter.
panelPlan: Single full-bleed portrait comic cover. No interior panel grid, no recap montage, no character-lineup poster, and no process or infographic framing.

Dominant selling image: Let landscape occupy most of the cover. The group is small in the lower foreground or middle distance, stopped on the road and looking toward a tiny unreadable Rider on a pale ridge. Use clear ridge layers and measurable-looking terrain so the reader instinctively trusts the geography. The Rider must be visually tiny but placed where the eye cannot stop returning.
Symbolic logic: The cover should look like an ordinary distance problem before the issue teaches the reader that distance may not behave honestly.

Thumbnail rule: the cover must still read at small size through one dominant silhouette or object relationship, a simple large-value composition, and a single obvious focal path. Do not depend on tiny props, background faces, or environmental lettering to explain the hook.

Trade-dress rule: reserve clean, intentional negative space for the established Sunforge Outlaw masthead, issue-number system, and any title treatment carried by the approved Issue 1 cover. Do not let important faces, hands, or the central symbolic object sit beneath the masthead zone.
Spoiler ceiling: Do not depict the Rider on multiple ridges, the failed approach, the later closer appearance, the morning silhouette behind them, or any overt spatial distortion.
Must include: vast negative space; one tiny Rider only; credible ridge geography; group scale emphasizing distance.
Must avoid: glow; spectral horse; motion blur; multiple Riders; warped horizon; portal or supernatural effects.

Dominant hook: A crowd of distinctive strangers looks like a conspiracy until you notice they are all busy with unrelated lives. Emotional promise: pattern recognition, humor, dense frontier culture, and a challenge to the travelers’ outsider assumptions.
settingText: Rookery crossroads near sunset; several roads, layered shade structures, carts, animals, market work, old dark structural fragments, constant ordinary movement.
panelPlan: Single full-bleed portrait comic cover. No interior panel grid, no recap montage, no character-lineup poster, and no process or infographic framing.

Dominant selling image: Use a slightly elevated crossroads view with Eva or Raina in the lower foreground studying several visually distinct people scattered through the Rookery. Arrange roads, awning poles, eyelines and structural fragments so the eye naturally connects the strangers into a false constellation, while each person is visibly doing an unrelated ordinary task. Marty should occupy a grounded central or counter-focal position as someone who actually knows the people.
Symbolic logic: The composition itself should tempt the reader into drawing connections that the town can explain.

title: Issue 11 Cover — What Jessie Left
summary: Cover for Sunforge Outlaw Issue 11, “What Jessie Left.” Shift the series’ emotional center to Jessie. The hook is not a wrong identity but a correct one—and the life she once left before anyone could decide it was permanent. Dominant hook: Jessie is caught between a place that genuinely knows her and the road she usually chooses before anyone can ask her to stay. Emotional promise: personal history, affection with teeth, choice rather than crisis, and a rare cover where recognition is correct.
settingText: Glasshouse courtyard in late-day light; old glass panels, familiar doorways, travel gear near a wall, open road visible beyond.
panelPlan: Single full-bleed portrait comic cover. No interior panel grid, no recap montage, no character-lineup poster, and no process or infographic framing.

Dominant selling image: Jessie stands near the visual hinge between the Glasshouse courtyard and the open road. One foot or shoulder can orient toward the road while her attention turns back toward the courtyard. Rachael is visible at a doorway or deeper in the familiar space, not as an antagonist but as proof that Jessie belonged here once. Keep Brandon off the focal axis.
Symbolic logic: The cover is a physical choice between a known place and an open road, without telling us which Jessie will choose tonight.
